extraction_notes.note: Theorem 1.1 is the classical cited Wedderburn-Artin theorem (external); the paper proves the prime-ring generalization Theorem 3.1, linked by a specializes edge.
Examples 2.1 and 2.5 contain definitions (M_n(D), standard matrix units) and proved assertions; these were emitted as nested definition/claim/proof nodes inside the example environments.

Historical remarks in the introduction (Wedderburn's finite-dimensional version, Artin's generalization) and the quaternion/field examples in the preliminaries were not made nodes; they are mentioned, not stated.

nodes.name: Wedderburn-Artin Theorem
nodes.statement: {\bf (Wedderburn-Artin Theorem)} If $R$ is a simple left artinian ring, then there exist a division ring $D$ and a positive integer $n$ such that $R\cong M_n(D)$.
nodes.statement_short: A simple left artinian ring is isomorphic to a full matrix ring over a division ring.
assumptions: $R$ is a simple left artinian ring
conclusions: there exist a division ring $D$ and a positive integer $n$ such that $R\cong M_n(D)$
nodes.label: AW

nodes.name: unity
nodes.statement: Our rings will be assumed to be unital, i.e., they contain an element $1$, called a unity, that satisfies $x=1x=x1$ for every ring element $x$.

nodes.name: left inverse
nodes.statement: An element $y$ is a left inverse of the element $x$ if $y x=1$.

nodes.name: right inverse
nodes.statement: A right inverse $z$ is defined analogously.

nodes.name: left and right inverses coincide
nodes.statement: If $x$ has both a left inverse $y$ and a right inverse $z$, then $y=y(xz)=(yx)z=z$. A left inverse of $x$ thus coincides with a right inverse of $x$.
assumptions: $x$ has both  a left inverse $y$ and a right inverse $z$
conclusions: $y=y(xz)=(yx)z=z$
A left inverse of $x$ thus coincides with a right inverse of $x$.

nodes.name: inverse
nodes.statement: We call it the inverse of $x$ and denote it by $x^{-1}$.

nodes.name: invertible element
nodes.statement: An element having an inverse is said to be invertible.

nodes.name: nonzero ring
nodes.statement: A ring is nonzero if $0$ is not its only element (equivalently, $0\ne 1$).

nodes.name: division ring
nodes.statement: A nonzero ring in which every nonzero element is invertible is called a division ring.

nodes.name: field
nodes.statement: A commutative division ring is called a field.

nodes.name: ring isomorphism
nodes.statement: A (ring) isomorphism is bijective map $\varphi$ from a ring $R$ to a ring $R'$ that satisfies $\varphi(a+b)=\varphi(a)+\varphi(b)$ and $\varphi(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)$ for all $a,b\in R$.

nodes.name: isomorphic rings
nodes.statement: We say that $R$ and $R'$ are isomorphic if there exists an isomorphism from $R$ to $R'$.

nodes.name: $R\cong R'$ notation
nodes.statement: In this case, we write $R\cong R'$.

nodes.name: left ideal / right ideal
nodes.statement: An additive subgroup $I$ of a ring $R$ is called a left ideal (resp. right ideal) if $u x\in I$ (resp. $xu\in I$) for all $u \in I$ and $x\in R$.
differentia: $u x\in I$ (resp. $xu\in I$) for all $u \in I$ and $x\in R$

nodes.name: ideal
nodes.statement: If $I$ is both a left and a right ideal, then it is called an ideal.

nodes.name: $Sa$, $aS$, $aSb$ notation
nodes.statement: For a subset $S$ of a ring $R$ and elements $a,b\in R$, write $Sa= \{sa\,|\,s\in S\}$, $aS=\{as\,|\,s\in S\}$, and $aSb=\{asb\,|\,s\in S\}$.

nodes.name: $RS$ notation
nodes.statement: By $RS$ we denote the set of all sums of elements of the form $xs$ with $x\in R$ and $s\in S$.

nodes.name: $RS$ is the left ideal generated by $S$
nodes.statement: Note that $RS$ is the left ideal of $R$ generated by $S$ (i.e., the smallest left ideal containing $S$).
conclusions: $RS$ is the left ideal of $R$ generated by $S$

nodes.name: $RaR$ is the ideal generated by $a$
nodes.statement: Taking $S=aR$, we obtain $RaR$ which is the ideal of $R$ generated by $a$.
assumptions: Taking $S=aR$
conclusions: $RaR$ which is the ideal of $R$ generated by $a$

nodes.name: product $IJ$ of left ideals
nodes.statement: If $I$ and $J$ are left ideals of $R$, then $IJ$ denotes the set of all sums of elements $uv$ with $u\in I$ and $v\in J$.

nodes.name: $IJ$ is a left ideal
nodes.statement: Observe that $IJ$ is again a left ideal (and is an ideal if $I$ and $J$ are ideals).
conclusions: $IJ$ is again a left ideal (and is an ideal if $I$ and $J$ are ideals)

nodes.name: $I^2$ notation
nodes.statement: If $I=J$, we write $I^2$ for $IJ$.

nodes.name: simple ring
nodes.statement: A nonzero ring $R$ whose only ideals are $\{0\}$ and $R$ is called a {\bf simple ring}.

nodes.name: division rings and matrix rings over division rings are simple
nodes.statement: (a) Obvious examples of simple rings are division rings, which do not even contain left (or right) ideals different from $\{0\}$ and $R$. This is because if a left ideal $I$ of any ring $R$ contains an invertible element $a$, then $I=R$. Indeed, $x=(xa^{-1})a\in I$ for every $x\in R$. (b) Let $D$ be a ring and $n\in \mathbb{N}$. The set of all $n\times n$ matrices with entries in $D$ is a ring under the usual matrix addition and multiplication. We denote it by $M_n(D)$ (for $n=1$, this is just $D$). Let $E_{ij}$ denote the matrix whose $(i,j)$ entry is $1$ and all other entries are $0$. We call $E_{ij}$, $1\le i,j\le n$, the {\bf standard matrix units}. By $aE_{ij}$ we denote the matrix whose $(i,j)$ entry is $a\in D$ and other entries are $0$. Observe that for every $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(D)$, \begin{equation*} E_{ij}AE_{kl} = a_{jk}E_{il}\quad\mbox{for all $1\le i,j,k,l\le n$.} \end{equation*} Now assume that $D$ is a division ring. Let $I$ be a nonzero ideal of $M_n(D)$. Take a nonzero $ (a_{ij})\in I$ and choose $j$ and $k$ such that $a_{jk}\ne 0$. From the displayed formula we see that $a_{jk}E_{il}\in I$ for all $i$ and $l$, and hence also $(d a_{jk}^{-1})E_{ii}\cdot a_{jk}E_{il} = dE_{il}\in I$ for every $d\in D$. Since every matrix in $M_n(D)$ is a sum of matrices of the form $dE_{il}$, $I=M_n(D)$. We have thus proved that $M_n(D)$ is a simple ring for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and every division ring $D$.
nodes.statement_short: Division rings and $M_n(D)$ over a division ring $D$ are simple; introduces matrix rings and standard matrix units.
nodes.label: ex21

nodes.name: division rings are simple
nodes.statement: Obvious examples of simple rings are division rings, which do not even contain left (or right) ideals different from $\{0\}$ and $R$.
conclusions: division rings, which  do not even contain left (or right) ideals different from  $\{0\}$ and $R$

nodes.name: proof that division rings have no proper nonzero left ideals
nodes.statement: This is because if a left ideal $I$ of any ring $R$ contains an invertible element $a$, then $I=R$. Indeed, $x=(xa^{-1})a\in I$ for every $x\in R$.
nodes.statement_short: A left ideal containing an invertible element $a$ is everything, since $x=(xa^{-1})a$.

nodes.name: matrix ring $M_n(D)$
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a ring and $n\in \mathbb{N}$. The set of all $n\times n$ matrices with entries in $D$ is a ring under the usual matrix addition and multiplication. We denote it by $M_n(D)$ (for $n=1$, this is just $D$).
differentia: of all $n\times n$ matrices with entries in $D$

nodes.name: $E_{ij}$
nodes.statement: Let $E_{ij}$ denote the matrix whose $(i,j)$ entry is $1$ and all other entries are $0$.

nodes.name: standard matrix units
nodes.statement: We call $E_{ij}$, $1\le i,j\le n$, the {\bf standard matrix units}.

nodes.name: $aE_{ij}$
nodes.statement: By $aE_{ij}$ we denote the matrix whose $(i,j)$ entry is $a\in D$ and other entries are $0$.

nodes.name: matrix unit sandwich identity
nodes.statement: E_{ij}AE_{kl} = a_{jk}E_{il}\quad\mbox{for all $1\le i,j,k,l\le n$.}
nodes.statement_short: Sandwiching $A$ between matrix units picks out the entry $a_{jk}$.
nodes.label: emu

nodes.name: proof that $M_n(D)$ is simple
nodes.statement: Now assume that $D$ is a division ring. Let $I$ be a nonzero ideal of $M_n(D)$. Take a nonzero $ (a_{ij})\in I$ and choose $j$ and $k$ such that $a_{jk}\ne 0$. From the displayed formula we see that $a_{jk}E_{il}\in I$ for all $i$ and $l$, and hence also $(d a_{jk}^{-1})E_{ii}\cdot a_{jk}E_{il} = dE_{il}\in I$ for every $d\in D$. Since every matrix in $M_n(D)$ is a sum of matrices of the form $dE_{il}$, $I=M_n(D)$.
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero ideal contains some $a_{jk}E_{il}$ by the sandwich identity, hence all $dE_{il}$, hence everything.

nodes.name: Take a nonzero ideal and a nonzero entry of one of its elements
nodes.statement: Now assume that $D$ is a division ring. Let $I$ be a nonzero ideal of $M_n(D)$. Take a nonzero $ (a_{ij})\in I$ and choose $j$ and $k$ such that $a_{jk}\ne 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a nonzero ideal and a nonzero entry of one of its elements.

nodes.name: Apply the matrix-unit identity to get all $dE_{il}$ in $I$
nodes.statement: From the displayed formula we see that $a_{jk}E_{il}\in I$ for all $i$ and $l$, and hence also $(d a_{jk}^{-1})E_{ii}\cdot a_{jk}E_{il} = dE_{il}\in I$ for every $d\in D$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the matrix-unit identity to get all $dE_{il}$ in $I$.

nodes.name: Every matrix is a sum of such, so $I$ is everything
nodes.statement: Since every matrix in $M_n(D)$ is a sum of matrices of the form $dE_{il}$, $I=M_n(D)$.
nodes.statement_short: Every matrix is a sum of such, so $I$ is everything.

nodes.name: $M_n(D)$ is simple
nodes.statement: We have thus proved that $M_n(D)$ is a simple ring for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and every division ring $D$.
assumptions: every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and every division ring $D$
conclusions: $M_n(D)$ is a simple ring

nodes.name: division rings are the only rings without proper nonzero left ideals
nodes.statement: If $a\ne 0$ is an element of a ring $R$ that does not have a left inverse, then the left ideal $Ra$ does not contain $1$ and is therefore different from $\{0\}$ and $R$. This readily implies that division rings are actually the only rings without proper nonzero left ideals. In particular, the ring $M_n(D)$ has proper nonzero left ideals for every $n\ge 2$.
nodes.statement_short: An element without left inverse generates a proper nonzero left ideal; so only division rings lack them, and $M_n(D)$ has them for $n\ge2$.

nodes.name: prime ring
nodes.statement: A ring $R$ is called a {\bf prime ring} if for all ideals $I$ and $J$ of $R$, $IJ=\{0\}$ implies $I=\{0\}$ or $J=\{0\}$.
differentia: for all ideals $I$ and $J$ of $R$, $IJ=\{0\}$ implies $I=\{0\}$ or $J=\{0\}$

nodes.name: simple rings and domains are prime
nodes.statement: Obviously, every simple ring is prime, and so is every ring without zero-divisors (i.e., a ring in which $ab=0$ implies $a=0$ or $b=0$).
conclusions: every simple ring is prime
so is every ring without zero-divisors

nodes.name: $\mathbb{Z}$ is prime but not simple
nodes.statement: The ring of integers $\mathbb{Z}$ is thus prime, but not simple since $n\mathbb{Z}$ is an ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: characterizations of prime rings
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a ring. The following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item[{\rm (i)}] $R$ is prime. \item[{\rm (ii)}] For all $a,b\in R$, $aRb =\{0\}$ implies $a=0$ or $b=0$. \item[{\rm (iii)}] For all left ideals $I$ and $J$ of $R$, $IJ=\{0\}$ implies $I=\{0\}$ or $J=\{0\}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Primeness via ideals, via $aRb=0$, and via left ideals are equivalent.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a ring.
conclusions: The following conditions  are equivalent:
equivalent_conditions: For all left ideals $I$ and $J$ of $R$, $IJ=\{0\}$ implies $I=\{0\}$ or $J=\{0\}$.
nodes.label: defprime

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement: (i)$\implies$(ii). Observe that $aRb=\{0\}$ yields $(RaR)(RbR)=\{0\}$, which by assumption implies $RaR=\{0\}$ and hence $a=0$, or $RbR=\{0\}$ and hence $b=0$. (ii)$\implies$(iii). If left ideals $I$ and $J$ satisfy $IJ=\{0\}$, then $aRb=\{0\}$ for every $a\in I$ and every $b\in J$. Therefore, by assumption, $a=0$ or $b=0$. (iii)$\implies$(i). Trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Cycle of implications (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii)$\Rightarrow$(i) via generated ideals.

nodes.name: (i) implies (ii) via the ideals $RaR$, $RbR$
nodes.statement: (i)$\implies$(ii). Observe that $aRb=\{0\}$ yields $(RaR)(RbR)=\{0\}$, which by assumption implies $RaR=\{0\}$ and hence $a=0$, or $RbR=\{0\}$ and hence $b=0$.
nodes.statement_short: (i) implies (ii) via the ideals $RaR$, $RbR$.

nodes.name: (ii) implies (iii) elementwise
nodes.statement: (ii)$\implies$(iii). If left ideals $I$ and $J$ satisfy $IJ=\{0\}$, then $aRb=\{0\}$ for every $a\in I$ and every $b\in J$. Therefore, by assumption, $a=0$ or $b=0$.
nodes.statement_short: (ii) implies (iii) elementwise.

nodes.name: (iii) implies (i) trivially
nodes.statement: (iii)$\implies$(i). Trivial.
nodes.statement_short: (iii) implies (i) trivially.

nodes.name: algebra over a field
nodes.statement: A ring $R$ is said to be an {\bf algebra} over a field $F$ if $R$ is also a vector space over $F$ and $\lambda(xy)=(\lambda x)y = x(\lambda y)$ holds for all $\lambda\in F$ and $x,y\in R$.
differentia: $R$  is also a vector space over $F$
$\lambda(xy)=(\lambda x)y = x(\lambda y)$ holds for all $\lambda\in F$ and $x,y\in R$

nodes.name: finite-dimensional algebra
nodes.statement: A finite-dimensional algebra is an algebra which is finite-dimensional as a vector space.

nodes.name: $M_n(F)$ as a finite-dimensional algebra
nodes.statement: The ring $M_n(F)$ becomes a finite-dimensional algebra if we endow it with the usual scalar multiplication $\lambda(a_{ij})=(\lambda a_{ij})$. The standard matrix units $E_{ij}$ form its basis, so its dimension is $n^2$.
nodes.label: eprvi

nodes.name: left artinian ring (descending chain condition)
nodes.statement: It is defined as follows: $R$ is a {\bf left artinian ring} (or is said to satisfy the {\bf descending chain condition} on left ideals) if for every descending chain $L_1\supseteq L_2\supseteq L_3\supseteq\dots$ of left ideals of $R$ there exists an $n_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $L_n=L_{n_0}$ for every $n\ge n_0$.
differentia: for every descending chain $L_1\supseteq L_2\supseteq L_3\supseteq\dots$ of left ideals of $R$ there exists an $n_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $L_n=L_{n_0}$ for every $n\ge n_0$
nodes.statement_short: Every descending chain of left ideals stabilizes.

nodes.name: examples of left artinian rings
nodes.statement: (a) Since a left ideal of an algebra is a vector subspace (because if $\lambda\in F$ and $u\in L$ then $\lambda u = (\lambda 1)u\in L$), a finite-dimensional algebra is indeed left-artinian. (b) Another obvious example of a left artinian ring is every division ring. Indeed, we saw above that such a ring does not even have proper nonzero left ideals. We claim that, more generally, the matrix ring $M_n(D)$ is left artinian for every $n\in \mathbb{N}$ and every division ring $D$. If $D$ is commutative, this follows from (a) and Example \ref{eprvi}. It turns out that essentially the same proof works if $D$ is not commutative. We omit details, but only indicate why this is true. One defines a vector space over a division ring in exactly the same way as a vector space over a field (but we call it more precisely a left vector space), and shows that every such vector space has a basis and that all bases have the same cardinality. This enables one to define the concept of dimension in the usual way. Now, the ring $M_n(D)$ is a vector space of dimension $n^2$ over $D$, and its left ideals are automatically vector subspaces. This implies that $M_n(D)$ is left artinian. (Incidentally, we do not define algebras over noncommutative division rings, so $M_n(D)$ is a ring and a vector space over $D$, but not an algebra over $D$.) (c) Being left artinian is a rather special property of a ring. For example, the ring $\mathbb{Z}$ has an infinite strictly descending chain of ideals $\mathbb{Z}\supsetneq 2\mathbb{Z} \supsetneq 4\mathbb{Z} \supsetneq 8\mathbb{Z} \supsetneq \dots $
nodes.statement_short: Finite-dimensional algebras, division rings and $M_n(D)$ are left artinian; $\mathbb{Z}$ is not.
nodes.label: eprvia

nodes.name: finite-dimensional algebras are left artinian
nodes.statement: Since a left ideal of an algebra is a vector subspace (because if $\lambda\in F$ and $u\in L$ then $\lambda u = (\lambda 1)u\in L$), a finite-dimensional algebra is indeed left-artinian.
conclusions: a finite-dimensional algebra is indeed left-artinian

conclusions: the matrix  ring $M_n(D)$ is  left artinian

nodes.name: simple left artinian converse
nodes.statement: The ring $M_n(D)$ is thus simple and left artinian. The Wedderburn-Artin Theorem states that the converse of this observation is true.

nodes.name: right artinian rings
nodes.statement: A right artinian ring is defined analogously via right ideals. However, we will consider only left artinian rings. This is just a matter of choice, the treatment of right artinian rings is essentially no different. In particular, we can substitute right for left in Theorem \ref{AW}. (A non-simple left artinian ring, however, is not always right artinian.)
nodes.statement_short: Right artinian rings are analogous; the theorem holds with right for left.

nodes.name: idempotent
nodes.statement: An element $e$ of a ring $R$ is called an {\bf idempotent} if $e^2=e$.

nodes.name: orthogonal idempotents
nodes.statement: Idempotents $e$ and $f$ are said to be {\bf orthogonal} if $ef=fe=0$.

nodes.name: sum of orthogonal idempotents is idempotent
nodes.statement: In this case, $e+f$ is also an idempotent.
conclusions: $e+f$ is  also an idempotent

nodes.name: examples of orthogonal idempotents
nodes.statement: (a) The simplest pair of orthogonal idempotents is $0,1$. An idempotent different from $0$ and $1$ is called a {\bf nontrivial idempotent}. (b) If $e$ is an idempotent, then so is $1-e$, and $e$ and $1-e$ are orthogonal. (c) The standard matrix units $E_{11},E_{22},\dots, E_{nn}$ are pairwise orthogonal idempotents.

nodes.name: nontrivial idempotent
nodes.statement: An idempotent different from $0$ and $1$ is called a {\bf nontrivial idempotent}.

nodes.name: strict inclusion of left ideals from orthogonal idempotents
nodes.statement: If $e$ and $f\ne 0$ are orthogonal idempotents in a ring $R$, then $R(1-e)\supsetneq R(1-e-f)$.
assumptions: $e$ and  $f\ne 0$ are  orthogonal idempotents in a ring $R$
conclusions: $R(1-e)\supsetneq R(1-e-f)$
nodes.label: l21

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 2.9
nodes.statement: Note that $(1-e-f)(1-e)= 1-e-f$, and hence $$x(1-e-f)=x(1-e-f)(1-e)\in R(1-e)$$ for every $x\in R$. This proves that $R(1-e)\supseteq R(1-e-f)$. We have $f=f(1-e)\in R(1-e)$, while $f=x(1-e-f)$ with $x\in R$ implies $$0=f(1-f)=x(1-e-f)(1-f)= x(1-e-f) = f,$$ a contradiction. Therefore, $R(1-e)\ne R(1-e-f)$.
nodes.statement_short: Inclusion from $(1-e-f)(1-e)=1-e-f$; strictness since $f\in R(1-e)$ but $f\in R(1-e-f)$ forces $f=0$.

nodes.name: Show the inclusion
nodes.statement: Note that $(1-e-f)(1-e)= 1-e-f$, and hence $$x(1-e-f)=x(1-e-f)(1-e)\in R(1-e)$$ for every $x\in R$. This proves that $R(1-e)\supseteq R(1-e-f)$.
nodes.statement_short: Show the inclusion.

nodes.name: Show strictness by contradiction using $f$
nodes.statement: We have $f=f(1-e)\in R(1-e)$, while $f=x(1-e-f)$ with $x\in R$ implies $$0=f(1-f)=x(1-e-f)(1-f)= x(1-e-f) = f,$$ a contradiction. Therefore, $R(1-e)\ne R(1-e-f)$.
nodes.statement_short: Show strictness by contradiction using $f$.

nodes.name: corner ring $eRe$
nodes.statement: If $e$ is an idempotent in a ring $R$, then $eRe$ is clearly a ring with unity $e$.
assumptions: $e$ is an idempotent in a ring $R$
conclusions: $eRe$ is clearly a ring with unity $e$

nodes.name: corner rings inherit artinian and prime
nodes.statement: Let $e$ be an idempotent in a ring $R$. \begin{enumerate} \item [{\rm (a)}] If $R$ is left artinian, then so is $eRe$. \item [{\rm (b)}] If $R$ is prime, then so is $eRe$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $e$ be an idempotent in a ring $R$.
$R$ is left artinian
$R$ is prime
conclusions: so is $eRe$

assumptions: $R$ is left artinian
conclusions: so is $eRe$

assumptions: $R$ is prime
conclusions: so is $eRe$

nodes.label: l23

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 2.10
nodes.statement: (a) Let $L_1\supseteq L_2 \supseteq L_3\supseteq\dots$ be a chain of left ideals of $eRe$. Then $RL_1\supseteq RL_2 \supseteq RL_3\supseteq\dots$ is a chain of left ideals of $R$. Since $R$ is left artinian, there exists an $n_0\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $RL_n = RL_{n_0}$, and hence $eRL_n = eRL_{n_0}$, for every $n\ge n_0$. However, since $L_n$ is a left ideal of $eRe$, $eRL_n = L_n$ for each $n$. Therefore, $L_n = L_{n_0}$ for $n\ge n_0$. (b) We verify that $eRe$ satisfies condition (ii) of Lemma \ref{defprime}. Let $eae,ebe\in eRe$ be such that $(eae)eRe(ebe)=\{0\}$. Since $R$ is prime, it follows that $eae=(eae)e=0$ or $ebe=e(ebe)=0$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (a) Lift chains via $L\mapsto RL$ and recover $L=eRL$; (b) check condition (ii) of Lemma 2.3.

nodes.name: Artinian part via chains $RL_n$
nodes.statement: (a) Let $L_1\supseteq L_2 \supseteq L_3\supseteq\dots$ be a chain of left ideals of $eRe$. Then $RL_1\supseteq RL_2 \supseteq RL_3\supseteq\dots$ is a chain of left ideals of $R$. Since $R$ is left artinian, there exists an $n_0\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $RL_n = RL_{n_0}$, and hence $eRL_n = eRL_{n_0}$, for every $n\ge n_0$. However, since $L_n$ is a left ideal of $eRe$, $eRL_n = L_n$ for each $n$. Therefore, $L_n = L_{n_0}$ for $n\ge n_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Artinian part via chains $RL_n$.

nodes.name: Prime part via condition (ii)
nodes.statement: (b) We verify that $eRe$ satisfies condition (ii) of Lemma \ref{defprime}. Let $eae,ebe\in eRe$ be such that $(eae)eRe(ebe)=\{0\}$. Since $R$ is prime, it follows that $eae=(eae)e=0$ or $ebe=e(ebe)=0$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Prime part via condition (ii).

nodes.name: minimal left ideal
nodes.statement: A nonzero left ideal $L$ of a ring $R$ is called a {\bf minimal left ideal} if $L$ does not properly contain a nonzero left ideal of $R$. That is to say, if $I$ is a left ideal such that $I\subseteq L$, then $I=\{0\}$ or $I=L$.
nodes.genus: nonzero left ideal $L$ of a ring $R$
differentia: $L$ does not properly contain a  nonzero left ideal of $R$

nodes.name: column left ideals of $M_n(D)$
nodes.statement: Let $R=M_n(D)$ with $D$ a division ring, and let $L$ be the set of matrices in $R$ that have arbitrary entries in the $i$th column and zeros in all other columns. It is an easy exercise to show that $L$ is a minimal left ideal of $R$. Observe that $L = RE_{ii}$ where $E_{ii}$ is the standard matrix unit, and $E_{ii}RE_{ii} = \{dE_{ii}\,|\, d\in D\}$, so $E_{ii}RE_{ii}\cong D$.
nodes.statement_short: Matrices supported in one column form a minimal left ideal $RE_{ii}$ of $M_n(D)$, with $E_{ii}RE_{ii}\cong D$.
nodes.label: ex332

nodes.name: minimal left ideal generated by idempotent with division corner
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a minimal left ideal of a ring $R$. If $L^2\ne \{0\}$, then there exists an idempotent $e\in L$ such that $L=Re$ and $eR e$ is a division ring.
nodes.statement_short: A minimal left ideal with nonzero square is $Re$ for an idempotent $e$ with $eRe$ a division ring.
assumptions: Let  $L$ be a  minimal left ideal of a ring $R$.
conclusions: there exists an idempotent $e\in L$ such that $L=Re$ and $eR e$ is a division ring
nodes.label: LD

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 2.12
nodes.statement:
By assumption, there exists a $y\in L$ such that $L y
e \{0\}$. As $L y$ is a left ideal of $R$ contained in $L$, $L y =L$ since $L$ is minimal. Therefore, there exists an $e\in L$ such that $ey =y$. Hence, $e^2 y = ey$, meaning that $e^2-e$ lies in the set $ J = \{z\in L \,|\, zy=0\}.$ Observe that $ J$ is a left ideal of $R$ contained in $L$. Since $Ly
e \{0\}$ and so $J
e L$, it follows that $J =\{0\}$. In particular, $e^2=e$. We have $R e\subseteq L$ since $e\in L$, and since $0
e e\in R e$ it follows from the minimality assumption that $L=R e$. Now consider the ring $eR e$. Let $a\in R$ be such that $eae
e 0$. We must prove that $eae$ is invertible in $eR e$. We have $\{0\}
e R eae \subseteq R e =L$, and so $R eae =L$. Hence, $beae = e$ for some $b\in R$, which gives $(ebe)(eae)=e$. Since $ebe$ is a nonzero element in $eR e$, by the same argument there exists a $c\in R$ such that $(ece)(ebe)=e$. But a left inverse coincides with a right inverse, so $eae = ece$ is invertible in $eRe$, with inverse $ebe$.
nodes.statement_short: Use minimality to find $e$ with $ey=y$, show $e$ is idempotent via an annihilator ideal, then invert nonzero $eae$ using minimality again.

nodes.name: Pick $y$ with $Ly=L$ by minimality
nodes.statement: By assumption, there exists a $y\in L$ such that $L y\ne \{0\}$. As $L y$ is a left ideal of $R$ contained in $L$, $L y =L$ since $L$ is minimal.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $y$ with $Ly=L$ by minimality.

nodes.name: Choose $e$ with $ey=y$ and the annihilator $J$
nodes.statement: Therefore, there exists an $e\in L$ such that $ey =y$. Hence, $e^2 y = ey$, meaning that $e^2-e$ lies in the set $ J = \{z\in L \,|\, zy=0\}.$
nodes.statement_short: Choose $e$ with $ey=y$ and the annihilator $J$.

nodes.name: Minimality kills $J$, so $e$ is idempotent
nodes.statement: Observe that $ J$ is a left ideal of $R$ contained in $L$. Since $Ly\ne \{0\}$ and so $J\ne L$, it follows that $J =\{0\}$. In particular, $e^2=e$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality kills $J$, so $e$ is idempotent.

nodes.name: Minimality gives $L=Re$
nodes.statement: We have $R e\subseteq L$ since $e\in L$, and since $0\ne e\in R e$ it follows from the minimality assumption that $L=R e$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality gives $L=Re$.

nodes.name: Reduce to inverting a nonzero $eae$
nodes.statement: Now consider the ring $eR e$. Let $a\in R$ be such that $eae\ne 0$. We must prove that $eae$ is invertible in $eR e$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to inverting a nonzero $eae$.

nodes.name: Minimality gives left inverses $ebe$ of $eae$ and $ece$ of $ebe$
nodes.statement: We have $\{0\}\ne R eae \subseteq R e =L$, and so $R eae =L$. Hence, $beae = e$ for some $b\in R$, which gives $(ebe)(eae)=e$. Since $ebe$ is a nonzero element in $eR e$, by the same argument there exists a $c\in R$ such that $(ece)(ebe)=e$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality gives left inverses $ebe$ of $eae$ and $ece$ of $ebe$.

nodes.name: Left and right inverses coincide
nodes.statement: But a left inverse coincides with a right inverse, so $eae = ece$ is invertible in $eRe$, with inverse $ebe$.
nodes.statement_short: Left and right inverses coincide.

nodes.name: $\mathbb{Z}$ has no minimal ideal
nodes.statement: Not every ring has a minimal left ideal. For example, the nonzero ideals of the ring $\mathbb{Z}$ are $n\mathbb{Z}$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and none of them is minimal since, say, $2n\mathbb{Z}\subsetneq n\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.name: existence of minimal left ideals in artinian rings
nodes.statement: A nonzero left artinian ring $R$ has a minimal left ideal.
assumptions: A nonzero left artinian ring $R$
conclusions: has a minimal left ideal
nodes.label: leftmi

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 2.14
nodes.statement: Choose a nonzero left ideal $L_1$ of $R$ (e.g., $L_1=R$). If $L_1$ is not minimal, there exists a nonzero left ideal $L_2$ such that $L_1\supsetneq L_2$. If $L_2$ is not minimal, then $L_2\supsetneq L_3$ for some nonzero left ideal $L_3$. Continuing this process we arrive in a finite number of steps at a minimal left ideal; for if not, there would exist an infinite chain $L_1\supsetneq L_2\supsetneq L_3\supsetneq \dots$
nodes.statement_short: Descend through nonzero left ideals; the descending chain condition stops the descent at a minimal one.

nodes.name: Build a strictly descending chain of nonzero left ideals
nodes.statement: Choose a nonzero left ideal $L_1$ of $R$ (e.g., $L_1=R$). If $L_1$ is not minimal, there exists a nonzero left ideal $L_2$ such that $L_1\supsetneq L_2$. If $L_2$ is not minimal, then $L_2\supsetneq L_3$ for some nonzero left ideal $L_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Build a strictly descending chain of nonzero left ideals.

nodes.name: The chain must stop at a minimal left ideal
nodes.statement: Continuing this process we arrive in a finite number of steps at a minimal left ideal; for if not, there would exist an infinite chain $L_1\supsetneq L_2\supsetneq L_3\supsetneq \dots$
nodes.statement_short: The chain must stop at a minimal left ideal.

nodes.name: set of $n\times n$ matrix units
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a ring and let $n\in\mathbb{N}$. We call $\{e_{ij}\in R \,|\,1\le i,j\le n\}$ a {\bf set of $n\times n$ matrix units} if $$e_{11}+e_{22}+\dotsb+e_{nn} = 1\quad\mbox{and}\quad e_{ij}e_{kl}=\delta_{jk}e_{il}$$ for all $1\le i,j,k,l\le n$. Here, $\delta_{jk}$ stands for the Kronecker delta.
nodes.statement_short: Elements $e_{ij}$ summing (diagonally) to 1 and multiplying like standard matrix units.

nodes.name: standard matrix units are matrix units
nodes.statement: By taking the identity matrix for $A$ in the displayed formula in Example \ref{ex21}\,(b) we see that the standard matrix units $E_{ij}$ are indeed matrix units of $M_n(D)$. There are others. For example, if $S\in M_n(D)$ is invertible, then $SE_{ij}S^{-1}$ are also matrix units.

nodes.name: diagonal corners are isomorphic
nodes.statement: If $e_{ij}$ are matrix units, then each ring $e_{ii}Re_{ii}$ is isomorphic to $e_{11}Re_{11}$. Indeed, it is an easy exercise to verify that $$e_{ii}ae_{ii}\mapsto e_{1i}(e_{ii}ae_{ii})e_{i1} = e_{11}(e_{1i}ae_{i1})e_{11}$$ is an isomorphism. Although not directly used in our proof of the Wedderburn-Artin Theorem, this helps in understanding it better. In particular, it explains why the next lemma involves $e_{11}Re_{11}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugation by $e_{1i}, e_{i1}$ identifies each corner $e_{ii}Re_{ii}$ with $e_{11}Re_{11}$.
nodes.label: reim

nodes.name: matrix units give a matrix ring
nodes.statement: If a ring $R$ contains a set of $n\times n$ matrix units $e_{ij}$, then $R\cong M_n(e_{11}R e_{11})$.
assumptions: a  ring $R$ contains a set of $n\times n$ matrix  units  $e_{ij}$
nodes.label: LMU

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 2.17
nodes.statement: For every $a\in R$, write $a_{ij} = e_{1i}ae_{j1}$. Observe that $a_{ij} = e_{11}a_{ij} e_{11} \in e_{11}R e_{11}$. Define $\varphi:R\to M_n(e_{11}R e_{11})$ by $$\varphi(a)=(a_{ij}). $$ Our goal is to show that $\varphi$ is an isomorphism. It is clear that $\varphi(a+b)=\varphi(a)+\varphi(b)$ for all $a,b\in R$. The $(i,j)$ entry of $\varphi(a)\varphi(b)$ is equal to $$\sum_{k=1}^n e_{1i}ae_{k1}e_{1k}be_{j1} =e_{1i}a\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^n e_{kk}\Bigr)be_{j1} = e_{1i}abe_{j1},$$ which is the $(i,j)$ entry of $\varphi(ab)$. Therefore, $\varphi(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)$. If $a_{ij}=0$ for all $i,j$, then $e_{ii}ae_{jj} = e_{i1}a_{ij}e_{1j} =0$, and so $a=0$ since the sum of all $e_{ii}$ is $1$. Thus, $\varphi$ is injective. Finally, observe that $\varphi(e_{k1}ae_{1l})$ is the matrix whose $(k,l)$ entry is $e_{11}ae_{11}$ and all other entries are $0$. Since every matrix in $M_n(e_{11}R e_{11})$ is a sum of such matrices, $\varphi$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: The map $a\mapsto(e_{1i}ae_{j1})$ is checked to be additive, multiplicative, injective and surjective.

nodes.name: Define the candidate map $\varphi$
nodes.statement: For every $a\in R$, write $a_{ij} = e_{1i}ae_{j1}$. Observe that $a_{ij} = e_{11}a_{ij} e_{11} \in e_{11}R e_{11}$. Define $\varphi:R\to M_n(e_{11}R e_{11})$ by $$\varphi(a)=(a_{ij}). $$ Our goal is to show that $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Define the candidate map $\varphi$.

nodes.name: Additivity and multiplicativity via $\sum e_{kk}=1$
nodes.statement: It is clear that $\varphi(a+b)=\varphi(a)+\varphi(b)$ for all $a,b\in R$. The $(i,j)$ entry of $\varphi(a)\varphi(b)$ is equal to $$\sum_{k=1}^n e_{1i}ae_{k1}e_{1k}be_{j1} =e_{1i}a\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^n e_{kk}\Bigr)be_{j1} = e_{1i}abe_{j1},$$ which is the $(i,j)$ entry of $\varphi(ab)$. Therefore, $\varphi(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)$.
nodes.statement_short: Additivity and multiplicativity via $\sum e_{kk}=1$.

nodes.name: Injectivity
nodes.statement: If $a_{ij}=0$ for all $i,j$, then $e_{ii}ae_{jj} = e_{i1}a_{ij}e_{1j} =0$, and so $a=0$ since the sum of all $e_{ii}$ is $1$. Thus, $\varphi$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity.

nodes.name: Surjectivity
nodes.statement: Finally, observe that $\varphi(e_{k1}ae_{1l})$ is the matrix whose $(k,l)$ entry is $e_{11}ae_{11}$ and all other entries are $0$. Since every matrix in $M_n(e_{11}R e_{11})$ is a sum of such matrices, $\varphi$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity.

nodes.name: extending partial matrix units
nodes.statement: If a ring $R$ contains pairwise orthogonal idempotents $e_{ii}$, $i=1,\dots,n$, whose sum is $1$, and elements $e_{1i}\in e_{11}Re_{ii}$ and $e_{i1} \in e_{ii}Re_{11}$, $i=2,\dots,n$, satisfying $e_{1i}e_{i1} = e_{11}$ and $e_{i1}e_{1i} = e_{ii}$, then the set $\{e_{ii}, e_{1i},e_{i1}\,|,i=1,\dots,n\}$ can be extended to a set of $n\times n$ matrix units. Accordingly, $R\cong M_n(e_{11}R e_{11})$.
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonal idempotents summing to 1 plus off-diagonal connectors $e_{1i},e_{i1}$ extend to matrix units, so $R\cong M_n(e_{11}Re_{11})$.
assumptions: a  ring $R$ contains pairwise orthogonal idempotents $e_{ii}$, $i=1,\dots,n$,  whose sum is  $1$
elements $e_{1i}\in e_{11}Re_{ii}$ and $e_{i1} \in e_{ii}Re_{11}$, $i=2,\dots,n$,  satisfying $e_{1i}e_{i1} = e_{11}$ and $e_{i1}e_{1i} = e_{ii}$
conclusions: the set $\{e_{ii}, e_{1i},e_{i1}\,|,i=1,\dots,n\}$ can be extended to a set of $n\times n$ matrix units
Accordingly, $R\cong M_n(e_{11}R e_{11})$.
nodes.label: fajnr

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 2.18
nodes.statement: For $i\ne j$ and $i,j\ne 1$, define $e_{ij} = e_{i1}e_{1j}$. Observe that our assumptions imply that $e_{ij} = e_{i1}e_{1j}$ holds in any case, that is, also if $i=j$ or one of $i,j$ is $1$. Note also that $e_{1j}e_{k1}=\delta_{jk}e_{11}$ holds for all $j$ and $k$. Consequently, for all $i,j,k,l$ we have $$e_{ij}e_{kl} = e_{i1}e_{1j}e_{k1}e_{1l} = \delta_{jk}e_{i1}e_{11}e_{1l} =\delta_{jk}e_{i1}e_{1l} = \delta_{jk}e_{il},$$ proving that $e_{ij}$ are matrix units. Therefore, $R\cong M_n(e_{11}R e_{11})$ by Lemma \ref{LMU}.
nodes.statement_short: Set $e_{ij}=e_{i1}e_{1j}$ and verify the matrix-unit relations, then apply Lemma 2.17.

nodes.name: Define the remaining $e_{ij}$
nodes.statement: For $i\ne j$ and $i,j\ne 1$, define $e_{ij} = e_{i1}e_{1j}$. Observe that our assumptions imply that $e_{ij} = e_{i1}e_{1j}$ holds in any case, that is, also if $i=j$ or one of $i,j$ is $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the remaining $e_{ij}$.

nodes.name: Record $e_{1j}e_{k1}=\delta_{jk}e_{11}$
nodes.statement: Note also that $e_{1j}e_{k1}=\delta_{jk}e_{11}$ holds for all $j$ and $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Record $e_{1j}e_{k1}=\delta_{jk}e_{11}$.

nodes.name: Verify the matrix-unit relations
nodes.statement: Consequently, for all $i,j,k,l$ we have $$e_{ij}e_{kl} = e_{i1}e_{1j}e_{k1}e_{1l} = \delta_{jk}e_{i1}e_{11}e_{1l} =\delta_{jk}e_{i1}e_{1l} = \delta_{jk}e_{il},$$ proving that $e_{ij}$ are matrix units.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the matrix-unit relations.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.17
nodes.statement: Therefore, $R\cong M_n(e_{11}R e_{11})$ by Lemma \ref{LMU}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 2.17.

nodes.name: orthogonal idempotents with division corners in a prime ring
nodes.statement: Let $e, f$ be a pair of orthogonal idempotents in a prime ring $R$ such that $eRe$ and $fRf$ are division rings. Then: \begin{enumerate} \item[{\rm (a)}] There exist $u\in eRf$ and $v\in fRe$ such that $uv=e$ and $vu=f$. \item[{\rm (b)}] $(e+f)R(e+f)\cong M_2(eRe)$. \item[{\rm (c)}] $eRe\cong fRf$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: In a prime ring, two orthogonal idempotents with division-ring corners are connected by $u,v$ with $uv=e$, $vu=f$.
assumptions: Let $e, f$ be a pair of orthogonal idempotents in a prime ring $R$ such that $eRe$ and $fRf$ are division rings.
conclusions: There exist $u\in eRf$ and $v\in fRe$ such that $uv=e$ and $vu=f$.
$(e+f)R(e+f)\cong M_2(eRe)$.
$eRe\cong fRf$.
nodes.label: finallem

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 2.19
nodes.statement: (a) Using condition (ii) of Lemma \ref{defprime} twice we infer that $eafbe\ne 0$ for some $a,b\in R$. As $eRe$ is a division ring with unity $e$, there is a $c\in R$ such that $(eafbe)(ece)=e$. Thus, $u=eaf\in eRf$ and $v=fbece\in fRe$ satisfy $uv=e$. Suppose $vu\ne f$. Then $vu-f$ is a nonzero, and hence invertible element of the division ring $fRf$. Observe that $vuv = ve =v$ and therefore $(vu-f)v =0$. Multiplying this equation from the left by the inverse of $vu-f$, we arrive at a contradiction $v= fv=0$. Thus, $vu=f$. (b) Observe that $e_{11}=e$, $e_{12}=u$, $e_{21}= v$, $e_{22}= f$ form a set of $2\times 2$ matrix units of $(e+f)R(e+f)$, so we can apply Lemma \ref{LMU}. (c) Use Remark \ref{reim}.
nodes.statement_short: (a) Primeness gives $eafbe\ne0$; invert it in $eRe$ to build $u,v$, and $vu=f$ by invertibility in $fRf$. (b),(c) follow from Lemma 2.17 and Remark 2.16.

nodes.name: Construct $u,v$ with $uv=e$, $vu=f$
nodes.statement: (a) Using condition (ii) of Lemma \ref{defprime} twice we infer that $eafbe\ne 0$ for some $a,b\in R$. As $eRe$ is a division ring with unity $e$, there is a $c\in R$ such that $(eafbe)(ece)=e$. Thus, $u=eaf\in eRf$ and $v=fbece\in fRe$ satisfy $uv=e$. Suppose $vu\ne f$. Then $vu-f$ is a nonzero, and hence invertible element of the division ring $fRf$. Observe that $vuv = ve =v$ and therefore $(vu-f)v =0$. Multiplying this equation from the left by the inverse of $vu-f$, we arrive at a contradiction $v= fv=0$. Thus, $vu=f$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $u,v$ with $uv=e$, $vu=f$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.17 to the $2\times 2$ matrix units
nodes.statement: (b) Observe that $e_{11}=e$, $e_{12}=u$, $e_{21}= v$, $e_{22}= f$ form a set of $2\times 2$ matrix units of $(e+f)R(e+f)$, so we can apply Lemma \ref{LMU}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 2.17 to the $2\times 2$ matrix units.

nodes.name: Apply Remark 2.16
nodes.statement: (c) Use Remark \ref{reim}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Remark 2.16.

nodes.name: weakening the division ring assumption on $fRf$
nodes.statement: We also remark that we can replace the assumption that $fRf$ is a division ring by a milder assumption that $f\ne 0$ and $fRf$ has no nontrivial idempotents. This is because $uv=e$ with $u\in eRf$ and $v\in fRe$ implies $(vu)^2= v(uv)u=veu=vu$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices that $f\ne0$ and $fRf$ has no nontrivial idempotents, since $vu$ is an idempotent.

nodes.name: prime ring with division corners summing to 1 is a matrix ring
nodes.statement: If a prime ring $R$ contains pairwise orthogonal idempotents $e_1,\dots,e_n$ such that their sum is $1$ and $e_iRe_i$ is a division ring for each $i$, then $R\cong M_n(e_1Re_1)$.
assumptions: a prime ring $R$ contains pairwise orthogonal idempotents $e_1,\dots,e_n$
their sum is $1$
$e_iRe_i$ is a division ring for each $i$
conclusions: $R\cong M_n(e_1Re_1)$
nodes.label: lemaresz

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 2.20
nodes.statement: Write $e_{ii}$ for $e_i$. Applying Lemma \ref{finallem}\,(a) to the idempotents $e_{11}$ and $e_{ii}$, $i\ge 2$, we see that there exist elements $e_{1i}\in e_{11}Re_{ii}$ and $e_{i1}\in e_{ii}Re_{11}$ satisfying $e_{1i}e_{i1} =e_{11}$ and $e_{i1}e_{1i} =e_{ii}$. Therefore, $R\cong M_n(e_{11}Re_{11})$ by Lemma \ref{fajnr}.
nodes.statement_short: Use Lemma 2.19(a) to connect $e_{11}$ with each $e_{ii}$, then apply Lemma 2.18.

nodes.name: Build connectors by Lemma 2.19(a)
nodes.statement: Write $e_{ii}$ for $e_i$. Applying Lemma \ref{finallem}\,(a) to the idempotents $e_{11}$ and $e_{ii}$, $i\ge 2$, we see that there exist elements $e_{1i}\in e_{11}Re_{ii}$ and $e_{i1}\in e_{ii}Re_{11}$ satisfying $e_{1i}e_{i1} =e_{11}$ and $e_{i1}e_{1i} =e_{ii}$.
nodes.statement_short: Build connectors by Lemma 2.19(a).

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.18
nodes.statement: Therefore, $R\cong M_n(e_{11}Re_{11})$ by Lemma \ref{fajnr}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 2.18.

nodes.name: nonzero prime left artinian rings are simple
nodes.statement: On the other hand, it is interesting in its own right that nonzero prime left artinian rings are automatically simple.
conclusions: nonzero prime left artinian rings are automatically simple

nodes.name: Wedderburn-Artin Theorem for prime rings
nodes.statement: If $R$ is a nonzero prime left artinian ring, then there exist a division ring $D$ and a positive integer $n$ such that $R\cong M_n(D)$.
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero prime left artinian ring is a full matrix ring over a division ring.
assumptions: $R$ is a nonzero prime left artinian ring
conclusions: there exist a division ring $D$ and a positive integer $n$ such that $R\cong M_n(D)$
nodes.label: W1

nodes.name: proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement:
Since $R$ is left artinian, $R$ contains a minimal left ideal $L$ (by Lemma ef{leftmi}), and since $R$ is prime, $L^2
e \{0\}$ (by Lemma ef{defprime}). Lemma ef{LD} therefore implies that $R$ contains an idempotent $e_1$ such that $e_1Re_1$ is a division ring. By Lemma ef{l21} (applied to $e=0$), $R\supsetneq R(1-e_1)$. If $e_1
e 1$, then $(1-e_1)R(1-e_1)$ is a nonzero ring, which is also prime and left artinian by Lemma ef{l23}. We can thus repeat the argument from the beginning of the proof to conclude that $(1-e_1)R(1-e_1)$ contains an idempotent $e_2$ such that $e_2(1-e_1)R(1-e_1)e_2$ is a division ring. Observe that $e_2\in (1-e_1)R(1-e_1)$ implies that $e_1$ and $e_2$ are orthogonal. Therefore, $e_2(1-e_1)R(1-e_1)e_2 =e_2Re_2$ and $R(1-e_1)\supsetneq R(1-e_1-e_2)$ by Lemma ef{l21}. If $e_1+e_2
e 1$, the same argument shows that there exists an idempotent $e_3$ belonging to $(1-e_1-e_2)R (1-e_1-e_2) $, and hence orthogonal to $e_1$ and $e_2$, such that $e_3(1-e_1-e_2)R(1-e_1-e_2)e_3 =e_3Re_3$ is a division ring and $R(1-e_1-e_2)\supsetneq R(1-e_1-e_2-e_3)$. We continue this process, which must stop after finitely many steps since $R$ is left artinian. Therefore, there exist pairwise orthogonal idempotents $e_1,\dots,e_n\in R$ such that $e_iRe_i$ is a division ring and $e_1+\dots+e_n=1$. Lemma ef{lemaresz} now gives the desired conclusion that $R\cong M_n(e_1Re_1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly split off idempotents with division-ring corners from minimal left ideals; the artinian condition stops the process, and Lemma 2.20 assembles them into matrix units.

nodes.name: Get an idempotent $e_1$ with division corner from a minimal left ideal
nodes.statement: Since $R$ is left artinian, $R$ contains a minimal left ideal $L$ (by Lemma \ref{leftmi}), and since $R$ is prime, $L^2\ne \{0\}$ (by Lemma \ref{defprime}). Lemma \ref{LD} therefore implies that $R$ contains an idempotent $e_1$ such that $e_1Re_1$ is a division ring.
nodes.statement_short: Get an idempotent $e_1$ with division corner from a minimal left ideal.

nodes.name: Strict descent of left ideals
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{l21} (applied to $e=0$), $R\supsetneq R(1-e_1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Strict descent of left ideals.

nodes.name: Repeat inside the corner $(1-e_1)R(1-e_1)$
nodes.statement: If $e_1\ne 1$, then $(1-e_1)R(1-e_1)$ is a nonzero ring, which is also prime and left artinian by Lemma \ref{l23}. We can thus repeat the argument from the beginning of the proof to conclude that $(1-e_1)R(1-e_1)$ contains an idempotent $e_2$ such that $e_2(1-e_1)R(1-e_1)e_2$ is a division ring.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat inside the corner $(1-e_1)R(1-e_1)$.

nodes.name: New idempotents are orthogonal and the chain keeps descending
nodes.statement: Observe that $e_2\in (1-e_1)R(1-e_1)$ implies that $e_1$ and $e_2$ are orthogonal. Therefore, $e_2(1-e_1)R(1-e_1)e_2 =e_2Re_2$ and $R(1-e_1)\supsetneq R(1-e_1-e_2)$ by Lemma \ref{l21}. If $e_1+e_2\ne 1$, the same argument shows that there exists an idempotent $e_3$ belonging to $(1-e_1-e_2)R (1-e_1-e_2) $, and hence orthogonal to $e_1$ and $e_2$, such that $e_3(1-e_1-e_2)R(1-e_1-e_2)e_3 =e_3Re_3$ is a division ring and $R(1-e_1-e_2)\supsetneq R(1-e_1-e_2-e_3)$.
nodes.statement_short: New idempotents are orthogonal and the chain keeps descending.

nodes.name: Artinian condition stops the process
nodes.statement: We continue this process, which must stop after finitely many steps since $R$ is left artinian. Therefore, there exist pairwise orthogonal idempotents $e_1,\dots,e_n\in R$ such that $e_iRe_i$ is a division ring and $e_1+\dots+e_n=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Artinian condition stops the process.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.20
nodes.statement: Lemma \ref{lemaresz} now gives the desired conclusion that $R\cong M_n(e_1Re_1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 2.20.
